**From the camera's perspective the wind blows from left to right.** It comes
*from* the left-hand side of the frame and carries the smoke *toward and out of*
the right-hand side of the frame.

Two further points about that wind:

- It is a **cross-frame, lateral wind** — it runs broadly across the camera's
  line of sight, not toward the lens and not away into the background. The smoke
  slides sideways across the scene rather than growing toward the viewer or
  shrinking into the distance.
- There is a **small additional downward component**: the smoke also sinks and
  spreads slowly toward the foreground as it travels, so the true motion is
  left-to-right and very slightly downward/toward the camera. The horizontal
  left-to-right component is by far the dominant one.

hitting you on your left side and blowing away to your right.

1. **Sheets of smoke enter frame left and exit frame right.** Grey veils of

   right side, and always clears *before* the right side.

the left over the 11 seconds — confirmed by template-matching the tailgate, the
cab and the utility pole), and then measured the smoke's own motion.

Smoke is low-contrast and hard to track directly, so I measured it through a
"transmission" field: the local image contrast at every point divided by its
own time-median. That value falls where smoke thickens and rises where it
clears, giving a clean per-pixel smoke-density signal that ignores the static
scenery.

**Test 1 — arrival-time ordering across the frame (the decisive one).** I took
the smoke-density signal in vertical strips at five different image columns and
cross-correlated their time series. Every single pair shows the left-hand column
leading the right-hand column, with lags that grow monotonically with
separation:

| column pair | separation | lag | correlation | direction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| x=110 → x=250 | 140 px | +0.47 s | 0.97 | left → right |
| x=110 → x=400 | 290 px | +0.80 s | 0.94 | left → right |
| x=110 → x=550 | 440 px | +1.67 s | 0.93 | left → right |
| x=110 → x=700 | 590 px | +2.40 s | 0.89 | left → right |
| x=250 → x=700 | 450 px | +1.80 s | 0.90 | left → right |
| x=400 → x=700 | 300 px | +1.67 s | 0.87 | left → right |
| x=550 → x=700 | 150 px | +0.60 s | 0.95 | left → right |

Monotonically increasing lag with distance, at a consistent implied propagation
speed of roughly 250–300 px/s, is the signature of genuine advection. The smoke
pattern crosses the full 854-pixel frame in about three seconds.

**Test 2 — space–time slices.** Plotting image-x against time produces smoke
streaks that all slant down-and-to-the-right (later in time = further right).
Not one streak slants the other way.

**Test 3 — local texture correlation.** Correlating the smoke-density profile
between frames 0.33 s apart gives a positive (rightward) displacement in every
horizontal band of the image (y = 0 through y = 280) and at every column
position sampled (x = 130 through x = 680), typically +5 to +22 px/s of
small-scale drift on top of the faster bulk front. There is no region of the
frame where the smoke moves leftward.

**Test 4 — masked Lucas–Kanade optical flow**, restricted to low-gradient
smoke-only pixels, agrees in sign: horizontal velocity positive, vertical
velocity near zero.

- **Not a camera artifact.** The camera pans slowly *rightward*, which shifts
  scene content leftward and would bias the measurement *against* the result I

  left-to-right (x=150 leads x=400 by 0.60 s, correlation 0.96). The conclusion

- **Not a one-off gust.** Splitting the shot into three sub-windows

- **Not motion toward the camera.** Smoke approaching the lens would diverge —

bearing (northerly, westerly, and so on) from this shot alone. Stated in the
